source.title: NeuroInspect: Interpretable Neuron-based Debugging Framework through Class-conditional Visualizations
source.authors: Yeong-Joon Ju; Ji-Hoon Park; Seong-Whan Lee

record.tranche_reason: The framework uses individual neurons as units for ranking causes of classification errors and producing visualizations, but does not test the claim's neuron-pole shares or the other specified versions.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses neurons with multiple facets and applies neuron-based visualizations, but reports no audit of the share of neurons with one or more jobs, no held-out activation test of explanations, and no automated explanation score. Its human preference results compare visualization methods and do not measure how many jobs a neuron has.
record.test_reason: NeuroInspect uses individual penultimate-layer neurons of ResNet image classifiers as debugging units and reports its own method's performance (spurious-correlation mitigation, worst-class accuracy, human preference among visualization methods). It reports no share of neurons with one or more jobs, no held-out activation prediction for explanations, no automated explanation scoring, and no study of InceptionV1 or of attribution graphs. Its qualitative claim that neurons have multiple facets is illustrative, not a population measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that NeuroInspect does three things without extra data or changes to the network: it ranks the neurons responsible for errors via counterfactual explanations, visualizes them class-conditionally with CLIP-Illusion, and edits the decision layer. They report that this mitigates spurious correlations and improves worst-class accuracy. They also report that practitioners preferred CLIP-Illusion visualizations (80% versus 3.75% for standard feature visualization).
record.recipe_differences: Uses counterfactual feature adjustments, class-conditioned visualizations with CLIP, and decision-layer editing in image classifiers; it does not reproduce the cited neuron-pole audit or its explanation tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that CLIP-Illusion visualizations depend on prompt design and can be limited by domain misalignment; changing the class-conditioning weight γ also changes the prominence of class-specific features and neuron activation.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet-18 trained on ImageNet, the authors label penultimate-layer neuron 0 as representing long diagonal lines, multiple round holes and animal faces. They say its top-activated images imply concepts with distant semantics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some late-layer neurons in CNN image classifiers respond to several semantically distant visual concepts, which class-conditioned visualization can separate.

record.problems: The neuron-facet evidence is an illustrative visualization rather than a quantitative audit; the paper does not report a population estimate of neuron interpretability.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were retained: the human preference table measures preference among visualization methods, not the number of jobs represented by neurons or prediction of activations on held-out examples.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no one-job, two-job or not-understood shares.
No language models and no interpretability shares across models or scale.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and no test of pose or recursive generalization versus superposition.
No estimate of the interpretable-neuron share by tool or architecture. The human preference table compares visualizations; it does not count interpretable neurons.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
No test of whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on held-out inputs.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Vision CNN debugging paper (ResNet-18/50). Its statements that neurons are 'multifaceted' are motivation for the method, not a measured test of any version. The human evaluation (Table I) measures preference among visualization methods only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report the stated one-job, two-job, or not-understood shares.
Does not estimate comparable interpretability shares across models, architectures, or scale.
Does not examine InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or test the pose/recursive-generalization interpretation.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares across architectures or tools, or test the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Does not test attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons or compare them with a replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations derived from activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Visualized neuron 0 using feature visualization, real images, and class-conditioned CLIP-Illusion visualizations.
rows.measure: Qualitative visualized features attributed to the neuron
rows.value: The paper identifies long diagonal lines, multiple round holes, and animal faces as concepts represented by neuron 0; the figure also shows class-conditioned visualizations for water jets, bridges, animal faces, and objects with holes.
rows.note: This is a qualitative example of multiple visualized facets, not a measurement of the share of neurons with one main job or a test of any specified version.
rows.check: Single hand-picked ResNet-18 neuron (neuron 0) shown with several visual facets. It is a qualitative illustration supporting the authors' visualization method, not a measurement of neuron-job shares in a language model (V1/V2), nor a test of V3 (no InceptionV1 or pose analysis) or V4 (no interpretable-share estimate across tools or architectures). Keep as a fits_no_version finding.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
